args.topic: Tenant's notice of the landlord's noncompliance

content:
Neither option is open on what is known now. Ending the lease is not settled, and not paying rent is not known yet. Both are about ending the lease or holding back rent; neither makes the landlord do the repair itself.

Ending the lease over the repair: not settled.
If the landlord "materially fails" to fix the problem within 7 days after delivery of your written notice naming it and saying you intend to end the lease because of it, you may end the lease (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)). Your lease says the landlord shall maintain the air-conditioning (Lease Section 7.1), and you confirmed you did not cause the problem, so the landlord's duty is met.

The open point is rent. You confirmed you paid rent after you knew the AC was out. A tenant who "pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" waives ending the lease over it, "but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a)). The statute does not settle this:
- One reading: a problem still not fixed is a continuing noncompliance, so paying rent while it goes on does not waive ending the lease. Then this option is open.
- Other reading: the noncompliance is the failure to fix the problem you already knew of, so paying rent waived ending the lease over it, and only a new or different failure starts over. Then this option is closed.
The statute also does not define "materially" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)). It may turn on how serious the condition is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living in the unit, or on whether the duty is one 83.51(1) lists, whatever its size.

Not paying rent as a defense: not known yet.
If the landlord sues for possession over unpaid rent, you may defend on a "material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1)" once 7 days have passed after your written notice saying you intend not to pay rent because of the problem (Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)). A lease promise alone does not reach this defense. You confirmed the AC is not structure or plumbing, which is one way in (Fla. Stat. 83.51(1)(b)). The other is a building, housing, or health code where your unit is that requires the landlord to fix it (Fla. Stat. 83.51(1)(a)). This tool does not hold those codes. You can check: the city or county code enforcement office can say whether one covers this problem, and can inspect the unit. If a code covers it, this option is open; if not, it is closed. You confirmed no eviction case has been filed; once one is, a tenant raising "any defense other than payment" must pay the rent into the court registry (Fla. Stat. 83.60(2)).

What either option needs first.
You confirmed your portal request did not say you intend to end the lease or not to pay rent, so neither 7-day period has started. Each starts from a new written notice delivered to the landlord that names the problem and says one of those intentions. Then 7 days must pass after it is delivered.

How the notice is delivered matters. Your lease says a maintenance request "is not by itself a notice under Section 13.1" (Lease Section 7.2). Section 13.1 lists delivery by hand to the leasing office, certified mail, or e-mail to office@magnoliarow.example (Lease Section 13.1). The statute lists "mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(4)). The program counts your portal request as a delivered written notice because you confirmed it, but whether it counts is for you to check against Lease Section 13.1.

Your lease also treats "Loss of air-conditioning when the outside temperature is above 85 degrees" as an emergency, reported by calling the after-hours emergency line at (352) 555-0147 (Lease Section 7.2). That turns on the outside temperature, not the temperature in your room, which you can check.

Cases (printed above; each read an older version of the statute, and the program marks them not verified):

K.D. Lewis Enterprises Corp. v. Smith, 445 So. 2d 1032 (Fla. 5th DCA 1984), read the 1981 statute. Tenants withheld rent over poor maintenance and did not pay it into the court registry, so possession was ordered (at 1033); you have paid rent and no case is filed. The court said "it is necessary for the tenant to comply with section 83.56, Florida Statutes (1981)" to recover for the lost value of the premises (at 1037). On your facts, getting money back for a hot room would run through the 83.56 notice, which you confirmed did not state an intention. First Hanover v. Vazquez follows it; no printed case distinguishes it.

Lakeway Management Co. of Florida v. Stolowilsky, 527 So. 2d 950 (Fla. 3d DCA 1988), read the 1985 statute. Tenants stopped paying rent and raised constructive eviction, but their first written complaint came only after the landlord's three-day notice (at 951); you have paid and no notice has come. The court said the trial court "erred in permitting this defense to be raised" (at 951). On your facts it points to the written complaint coming first; it does not say whether a portal request is enough. No printed case distinguishes it.

Bennett v. Mattison, 382 So. 2d 873 (Fla. 1st DCA 1980), read the 1977 statute. A tenant fell in a common hallway; the court said "The violation of this statutory duty would be evidence of negligence." (at 875). It is about an injury in a common area, not an AC in your room, so it matters only if you are hurt. No printed case distinguishes it.

Solomon v. Gentry, 388 So. 2d 52 (Fla. 4th DCA 1980), read the 1979 statute. A tenant's heating unit was not working, was repaired, and then a fire destroyed the home's contents; the court held "no such warranty arises under a lease of real property" (at 53), meaning an implied warranty of fitness for a specific purpose. Alike: a broken climate unit. Different: fire damage. On your facts, a claim over your AC would rest on your lease (Lease Section 7.1) and the statute, not on that warranty. No printed case distinguishes it.

Mansur v. Eubanks, 401 So. 2d 1328 (Fla. 1981), read the 1977 statute. A tenant was hurt in a gas explosion; the court said the landlord has "a continuing duty to exercise reasonable care to repair dangerous defective conditions upon notice of their existence by the tenant" (at 1330). Whether a broken AC is a "dangerous" condition is not settled by your facts or by the case. K.D. Lewis distinguished it as not creating a new claim in tort for the lost value of the premises (at 1038), and Bennett M. Lifter read it as not excusing the landlord for conditions "not inherently dangerous" (at 1341).

Paterson v. Deeb, 472 So. 2d 1210 (Fla. 1st DCA 1985), read the 1981 statute. A tenant was attacked after the landlord left a lock broken and common areas dark; the court said "A landlord’s violation of the act is at least evidence of negligence." (at 1216). It is about injury from a crime, so it matters only if you are hurt. Menendez distinguished it: the duty in Paterson "was based on a violation of an express provision of the statute" (Menendez at 62).

Bennett M. Lifter, Inc. v. Varnado, 480 So. 2d 1336 (Fla. 3d DCA 1985), read the 1983 statute and a county code. A hot water heater was out for three days after a report and no one was sent, and a child was burned (at 1337). Alike: an appliance out after a report with no repair. Different: an injury, and hot running water, which the court tied to 83.51 (at 1341). The court said Mansur "did not purport to exonerate the landlord from responsibility for faulty injury-producing conditions which are not inherently dangerous" (at 1341). You described no injury. Smith v. Grove Apartments called itself virtually indistinguishable from it (Smith at 588).

Haynes v. Lloyd, 533 So. 2d 944 (Fla. 5th DCA 1988). A child was cut by broken glass on the ground at an apartment complex; the majority said the common-area duty in 83.51(2)(a) 3. "merely restates the landlord’s common law duty as it would exist in the absence of a statute" (at 945), and the dissent disagreed (at 947). Different: a common area and an injury. It says nothing on an AC in your unit. No printed case distinguishes it.

Ray v. Tampa Windridge Associates, 596 So. 2d 676 (Fla. 2d DCA 1991), read the 1985 statute. A tenant signed a security release, and the court found the landlord's duty to make reasonable provisions for locks "was dispensed with" only if the release did so, and it did not (at 677). Different: locks and an attack. Alike only in that a duty can turn on what the signed paper says; your lease's repair clause names air-conditioning (Lease Section 7.1), and nothing on your facts shows a release. No printed case distinguishes it.

Menendez v. Palms West Condo. Ass'n, 736 So. 2d 58 (Fla. 1st DCA 1999). A man was shot at his apartment door, which had no peephole; the court said the association could not be liable under the lease because "the lease contained no provision that either expressly or by implication required the installation of a doorscope" (at 62). Different: a crime, and a lease with no such clause. Your lease has a repair clause that names air-conditioning (Lease Section 7.1).

Smith v. Grove Apartments, LLC, 976 So. 2d 582 (Fla. 3d DCA 2007), read the 2007 statute. A tenant complained repeatedly about overgrown foliage, the landlord did nothing, and the tenant fell while trimming it himself (at 583). The court said "the landlord retained its statutory duty to maintain the parking lot area in a clean and safe condition" (at 586); a dissent would have found no duty to trim the branches (at 596). Alike: repeated complaints and no fix. Different: a common area and an injury. It decides nothing about an AC in your own unit.

None of these cases is about air-conditioning, and none printed above says a portal request is or is not the written notice the statute names.

On the portal request: it did not start either 7-day period. Each period needs a written notice that names the problem and says an intention, either to end the lease (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)) or not to pay rent (Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)). You confirmed your request said neither. It was still the way your lease says to report a repair (Lease Section 7.2), but that clause also says a maintenance request "is not by itself a notice under Section 13.1" (Lease Section 7.2). Neither the lease's list of delivery ways nor the statute's list names a portal (Lease Section 13.1; Fla. Stat. 83.56(4)).

What you would send and where. Neither option is open yet. Ending the lease is not settled: it turns on whether paying rent after you knew of the AC problem waived it (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a)). Not paying rent is not known yet: it turns on whether a building, housing, or health code where your unit is covers this problem, which the city or county code enforcement office can tell you. If the open point goes your way, the steps are:
- A written notice that names the AC problem and says you intend to end the lease because of it (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)), or says you intend not to pay rent because of it (Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)). A letter that only asks for the repair and states neither intention would not start either 7-day period.
- Delivered one of the ways your lease lists: by hand to the leasing office at 2600 SW Hartwell Lane, Gainesville, Florida 32608, by certified mail to that address, or by e-mail to office@magnoliarow.example (Lease Section 13.1). The statute lists "mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(4)). The rent notice may also go to the landlord's designated representative, a resident manager, or the person or entity who collects the rent (Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)).
- Then 7 days must pass after delivery with the problem still not fixed.

On not stopping rent: only the second option is about not paying rent. The first option does not ask you to stop, but your paying rent is the very point that is not settled for it. The statute does not settle this:
- One reading: a problem still not fixed is a continuing noncompliance, so paying rent while it goes on does not waive ending the lease. Then ending the lease is open.
- Other reading: the failure to fix the problem you already knew of is the noncompliance, so paying rent waived ending the lease over it, and only a new or different failure starts over. Then ending the lease is closed.
Your lease also gives a second route that involves no notice and no stopping rent: reporting loss of air-conditioning as an emergency when the outside temperature is above 85 degrees (Lease Section 7.2), which you can check against the outside temperature.

On eviction: the statute makes it unlawful for a landlord to "bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant". Its examples include a tenant who "has complained to the landlord pursuant to s. 83.56 (1)", and the tenant must have acted in good faith (Fla. Stat. 83.64(1)). The examples are not the whole list, and the statute text I have does not say whether a repair request like yours, with no intention stated, is covered. The protection does not apply if the landlord proves the eviction is for good cause, and the examples of good cause include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent" (Fla. Stat. 83.64(3)). You confirmed no eviction case has been filed.

Salmonte v. Eilertson, 526 So. 2d 179 (Fla. 1st DCA 1988), read 83.64(3) (no year stated). A tenant who had refused the landlords' inspections admitted keeping pets and other lease breaches; the landlords sued to evict and he raised retaliation (at 180). The court said "The tenant admitted breaching the lease." (at 180), and that the defense "could not be raised because Section 83.64(3), Florida Statutes, provides that the defense does not apply when the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause" (at 180). Different: you have admitted no breach and no case is filed, and that case involved lease violations, not unpaid rent. It cuts against you in one way: a retaliation defense can fail when the landlord proves good cause. No printed case distinguishes it.

You said e-mail, and your lease allows it: "sent by e-mail to office@magnoliarow.example" (Lease Section 13.1). Two things are still missing before the letter is drafted: how many days you give them to reply, and which kind of letter. The three kinds are:

preserve: "Describes the condition and asks for the repair. Cites nothing."
assert: "Adds the 83.51(1) duty, quoted."
escalate: "Adds the 83.56(1) sentence, quoted."

An assert letter would quote your lease's sentence "Landlord shall maintain in good working order and repair the heating, air-conditioning, plumbing, and electrical systems serving the Unit" (Lease Section 7.1); whether a code makes 83.51(1) reach an AC is not known yet. An escalate letter would quote the 83.56(1) sentence that ends "the tenant may terminate the rental agreement", which is about ending the lease, and you said you do not want to.

Which kind, and how many days to reply?

args.topic: Tenant's notice of the landlord's noncompliance

content:
Getting rent back is not one of the options the program checks, and the statute text I have does not settle it on your facts. It can come up three ways, and each turns on a point that is not decided yet.

1. Damages. "The aggrieved party may recover the damages caused by the noncompliance" when a landlord fails to comply with the rental agreement or this part (Fla. Stat. 83.55). Your lease says the landlord shall maintain the air-conditioning (Lease Section 7.1). This is not settled, because you confirmed you paid rent after you knew of the problem, and a tenant who does so waives the right "to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(5)(a)). The statute does not settle this:
- One reading: a problem still not fixed is a continuing noncompliance, so paying rent while it goes on does not waive a claim over it. Then this route is open.
- Other reading: the failure to fix the problem you already knew of is the noncompliance, so paying rent waived a claim over it, and only a new or different failure starts over. Then this route is closed.

2. A rent reduction. The statute says that where a failure is due to causes beyond the landlord's control, the landlord "has made and continues to make every reasonable effort", and the unit is still lived in, "the rent for the period of noncompliance shall be reduced by an amount in proportion to the loss of rental value caused by the noncompliance" (Fla. Stat. 83.56(1)(b)). Whether the delay for a part is beyond the landlord's control, and whether the landlord has made every reasonable effort, are not known yet. That sentence sits inside the one about a failure after a tenant's notice, and the statute text I have does not say whether it reaches a tenant whose notice stated no intention to end the lease.

3. A reduction as a defense, only if the landlord sues for possession over unpaid rent. Then "the amount, if any, by which the rent is to be reduced to reflect the diminution in value of the dwelling unit" is for the court or jury to decide (Fla. Stat. 83.60(1)(b)). This needs a failure of a duty in 83.51(1), which is not known yet (whether a code where your unit is covers an AC; the city or county code enforcement office can tell you), and a notice saying you intend not to pay rent, which you said you do not want to send.

Your lease points the other way on a reduction: "no such interruption entitles Resident to any reduction or abatement of Rent", for an "interruption or failure of utilities, internet, or other services caused by a provider, a repair, or anything beyond Landlord's reasonable control" (Lease Section 5.2). Whether an AC with a dead compressor is such a service is for you to check against that clause. The statute says a rental agreement provision is "void and unenforceable to the extent that it" "Purports to waive or preclude the rights, remedies, or requirements set forth in this part" (Fla. Stat. 83.47(1)(a)). So if a reduction is one of the statute's remedies on your facts, Lease Section 5.2 is void to that extent; if it is not, 5.2 is not what stands in the way.

How much: the tool does not work out an amount. Your rent is $789 per installment (Lease Section 3.1), but none of these sections sets a share of it for a room without AC. They speak of "damages caused by the noncompliance", a reduction "in proportion to the loss of rental value", and a "diminution in value" a court decides.

Cases (printed earlier in this chat; each read an older version of the statute and is marked not verified):

K.D. Lewis Enterprises Corp. v. Smith, 445 So. 2d 1032 (Fla. 5th DCA 1984), read the 1981 statute. Tenants withheld rent claiming the landlord did not maintain their apartments, and lost possession when they did not pay rent into the court registry (at 1033). The court said "To recover for diminishment in the value of the premises, it is necessary for the tenant to comply with section 83.56, Florida Statutes (1981)" (at 1037), and rejected recovering that loss "under a negligence theory" (at 1038). On your facts, a claim for the lost value of your room would run through the 83.56 notice, and you confirmed your notice did not state an intention to end the lease. Different: those tenants withheld rent, and you have paid. First Hanover v. Vazquez follows it; no printed case distinguishes it.

Lakeway Management Co. of Florida v. Stolowilsky, 527 So. 2d 950 (Fla. 3d DCA 1988), read the 1985 statute. Tenants who stopped paying rent raised constructive eviction, but their first written complaint came only after the landlord's three-day notice, and the court said the defense should not have been allowed (at 951). It is about the order of a written complaint and a defense in an eviction, so it says nothing on an amount, and you have paid rent with no eviction case filed. No printed case distinguishes it.

The maintenance cases printed earlier are about injuries and property damage, and none is about getting rent back.
